stops.title: Shielding the Wounded Deer at Saint-Gilles-du-Gard
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Abbaye de Saint-Gilles-du-Gard to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Sunlight filtering through tangled southern French oak woods into a mossy cave opening where a serene bearded hermit holds a trembling forest doe close while raising his own wounded hand calmly before an astonished royal hunter.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: UNESCO-listed **Abbey of Saint-Gilles-du-Gard**—boasting one of Europe’s most stunning sculpted stone Romanesque façades!—remains a major starting point along the southern **Via Tolosana** Camino route to Santiago de Compostela!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Because St. Giles took that arrow cheerfully and lived with a permanent physical disability—refusing miraculous healing so he could stay close to struggling people!—he became the beloved **Patron Saint of People with Physical Disabilities, Beggars, and Forest Animals!**
stops.saintQuote: Let no innocent creature be harmed where prayer makes its home.

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Shielding the Wounded Deer at Saint-Gilles-du-Gard
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Living peacefully inside a briar-hidden cave near the mouth of the Rhône River in southern France, Giles befriended a gentle wild **red deer (hind)** that visited his cave daily! One autumn afternoon, royal hunters chased the terrified deer straight into the brambles outside Giles’s cave and fired an arrow blindly through the bushes! Jumping straight in front of the frightened animal, Giles **caught the hunter’s arrow right through his own hand**—choosing a lifelong limp and injury so the helpless deer would live! Horrified and deeply moved by the hermit’s tender bravery, Visigothic King Wamba apologized humbly and built **Saint-Gilles Abbey** around his cave!

completionSummary: You walked from sunny medieval Sweden all the way to Jerusalem, Santiago, and Rome with fearless thirteenth-century pioneer St. Ingrid of Skänninge—the widowed noblewoman who made THREE epic cross-continental pilgrimages on foot before returning home to launch Sweden’s very first Dominican convent!

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Quiet historic **Skänninge** still treasures the medieval heritage of St. Ingrid—Sweden’s pioneering woman pilgrim who blazed the trail nearly a full century before St. Bridget of Sweden!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: St. Ingrid’s own brother **John Elovsson** was a knight of the Teutonic Order—and their close spiritual advisor was **Blessed Peter of Dacia**, celebrated as Sweden’s very first literary author!
stops.saintQuote: Open your heart to the road, and God will build a home wherever you walk.

stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Hierosolyma, Compostela & Roma to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Sun-warmed ancient stone pilgrim road outside Jerusalem’s golden walls where a determined Nordic woman pilgrim wearing a wool cloak and scallop shell gazes gratefully across the sunlit Holy City.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Historians marvel at St. Ingrid’s astonishing 13th-century stamina—covering well over **10,000 miles** by foot and medieval sailing ships between Scandinavia, Spain, Italy, and the Holy Land!

stops.title: Founding Sweden’s First Dominican Convent
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Sankt Martins kloster, Skänninge to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Tranquil northern brick cloister courtyard bathed in warm golden late-summer Scandinavian sunshine where white-robed sisters sing evening psalms together in joyful peace.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Across Scandinavia, St. Ingrid of Skänninge is warmly remembered every September 2 as one of medieval Sweden’s brightest stars of courage, scholarship, and spiritual hospitality.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Over two centuries later in 1507, Swedish bishops held a joyous ceremonial translation of St. Ingrid’s relics attended by cheering crowds across Sweden—celebrating her as one of Sweden’s great national patronesses!
stops.saintQuote: Finish the work entrusted to your hands, and peace will crown your days.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Returning home victorious to **Skänninge** with official Dominican and papal blessing, Ingrid inaugurated **St. Martin’s Convent** on August 15, 1281—with **King Magnus Ladulås of Sweden** himself attending in festive honor! Serving joyfully as its first Prioress, Mother Ingrid established a radiant Nordic center of women’s literacy, hospitality, and contemplative study—passing away peacefully just one year later on **September 2, 1282** with her life’s dream gloriously fulfilled!

stops.title: From Roman Mayor to Humble Monk on Caelian Hill
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Clivus Scauri (Caelian Hill, Rome) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: c. 540 – 590 · San Gregorio al Celio, Rome
stops.imageCaption: Warm golden sunlit Roman hillside abbey garden overlooking the ruins of the Palatine Palace where a former Roman governor happily sweeps stone steps in a humble dark wool tunic.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Standing proudly on Rome’s Caelian Hill, the graceful **Church of San Gregorio al Celio** still preserves the ancient marble table where St. Gregory personally fed twelve poor Roman beggars EVERY SINGLE DAY!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Legend remembers that one day while Gregory served twelve hungry guests at his Caelian Hill table, he looked up and counted **THIRTEEN**—realizing a smiling radiant angel had quietly sat down to dine among Rome’s poor!
stops.saintQuote: Servant of the Servants of God.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Born into a dazzlingly wealthy Roman senatorial family around 540, brilliant young **Gregory** rose by age thirty-three to become **Prefect (Mayor) of Rome**—wearing gleaming silk robes and running the crumbling Eternal City! Yet the day his father passed away, Gregory liquidated his sprawling Sicilian estates to build **six monasteries**, converted his OWN luxurious family palace on Rome’s **Caelian Hill** into **St. Andrew’s Monastery**, and joyfully traded velvet for a monk’s rough wool tunic—calling those quiet years his happiest days on earth!

detectiveClues.headline: From Roman Mayor to Humble Monk on Caelian Hill
detectiveClues.clueText: Born into a dazzlingly wealthy Roman senatorial family around 540, brilliant young **Gregory** rose by age thirty-three to become **Prefect (Mayor) of Rome**—wearing gleaming silk robes and running the crumbling Eternal City! Yet the day his father passed away, Gregory liquidated his sprawling Sicilian estates to build **six monasteries**, converted his OWN luxurious family palace on Rome’s **Caelian Hill** into **St. Andrew’s Monastery**, and joyfully traded velvet for a monk’s rough wool tunic—calling those quiet years his happiest days on earth!

stops.title: Gregorian Chant & "Not Angles, But Angels!"
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Schola Cantorum, Roma & Canterbury Mission to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: 596 – March 12, 604 · St. Peter’s Basilica & Mission to England
stops.imageCaption: Warm golden candlelit Roman choir loft where smiling young singers chant flowing sacred Latin melodies beside a thoughtful pope wearing a white dove perched quietly near his ear.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Named one of the four **Great Latin Doctors of the Church** (alongside Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine), Pope St. Gregory the Great is the universal **Patron Saint of Musicians, Singers, Students, and Teachers**!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: King Alfred the Great of England loved St. Gregory’s leadership book *Pastoral Care* so deeply that he personally translated it into Old English and mailed a copy to EVERY single cathedral in England!
stops.saintQuote: Not Angles, but Angels—let the Alleluia ring across their green hills!

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: Find the luminous focal point of Schola Cantorum, Roma & Canterbury Mission in the scene.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Scan the center-left horizon of the painting.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Gregorian Chant & "Not Angles, But Angels!"
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Wait until you hear the funniest pun in medieval history! Years earlier walking through Rome’s tragic slave market, Gregory had spotted fair-haired young boys being sold as slaves and asked where they came from. Told *"They are Angles (from England),"* Gregory smiled warmly: **"Not Angles—ANGELS!"** Never forgetting them, once Pope in 596 he sent forty monks from his own Caelian Hill abbey led by **St. Augustine of Canterbury** straight to England—launching English Christianity! Meanwhile in Rome, his passionate love of sacred liturgy and the *Schola Cantorum* gave the world **Gregorian Chant**—AND his brilliant guidebook ***Pastoral Care*** became the bestselling leadership handbook for bishops and kings across Europe for a thousand years!

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Stepping inside the **Sanctuary of Santa Rosalia** atop Mount Pellegrino is pure magic: the church literally has **NO artificial roof**—instead, the towering natural limestone cave ceiling drips glistening mineral water caught neatly in silver basins!

stops.saintQuote: In the quiet stone cleft above the sea, my soul rests completely free.

stops.title: Ending the 1624 Plague at Palermo Cathedral
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Cattedrale di Palermo to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Warm golden honey-stone Norman-Baroque cathedral glowing at twilight surrounded by cheering Sicilian crowds carrying cascading bouquets of summer roses.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Inside **Palermo Cathedral**, her gleaming 700-kilogram engraved silver urn glows year-round—and every July and September 4, thousands of Sicilians climb Mount Pellegrino barefoot through the starry night singing *"Viva Palermo e Santa Rosalia!"*
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Wait until you hear a wild biology fact named after St. Rosalia: in 1959 ecologist G. Evelyn Hutchinson stopped by Mount Pellegrino’s cave, spotted two tiny water-bug species thriving side by side in a shallow shrine pond, and published his world-famous biodiversity paper ***"Homage to Santa Rosalia, or Why Are There So Many Kinds of Animals?"***—making St. Rosalia an unexpected unofficial **Patron Saint of Evolutionary Biology!**
stops.saintQuote: Viva Palermo e Santa Rosalia!

On **June 9, 1625**, as joyful Palermitans carried her relics down the mountain in singing procession through every plague-stricken alley, the epidemic **stopped cold!**

stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Scupi (Skopje) to uncover 3 hidden memories

stops.imageCaption: Soaring twin asymmetrical Gothic cathedral spires rising dramatically above golden French wheat fields, glowing inside with iconic luminous Chartres sapphire-blue stained glass.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Gazing up at Chartres’s glowing 13th-century **"Blue Virgin"** stained-glass window—and walking its famous stone floor labyrinth—reminds every visitor that Mary’s birth still floods the world with sapphire light!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Because September 8 falls right at Europe’s early autumn grape and grain harvest, French winemakers even call September 8 **"Our Lady of the Grape Harvest"**—bringing the season’s first ripe clusters to church in gratitude!

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Across France and Europe, September 8 shines brightest at **Chartres Cathedral**—home since 876 AD to the treasured **Sancta Camisia**, an ancient silk veil venerated as Mary’s tunic gifted by Emperor Charles the Bald! Instantly, rich nobles and ordinary stonemasons alike harnessed themselves to stone wagons singing hymns—rebuilding soaring **Chartres Cathedral** in a breathtaking 26 years!

stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Kahlenberg & Stephansdom, Vienna to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Panoramic golden morning light rising over forested Vienna Woods vineyards overlooking the glittering Danube and the towering gothic spire of St. Stephen’s Cathedral as joyful bells ring across the valley.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Stand on panoramic **Kahlenberg Hill** overlooking Vienna’s vineyards and visit St. Joseph’s Church—AND remember the charming Viennese baking legend born that exact week: celebratory bakers shaped golden crescent rolls (**Kipferl** → later inspiring France’s **croissant!**) AND brewed beans left behind in the camps to launch **Vienna’s legendary Coffeehouse culture!**
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: In joyous gratitude for Vienna’s peaceful deliverance on September 12, 1683, Pope Blessed Innocent XI immediately extended the **Feast of the Most Holy Name of Mary** to the entire worldwide Church!
stops.saintQuote: We came, we saw—God conquered!

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Dawn Mass on Kahlenberg Hill & St. Stephen’s, Vienna
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Originally celebrated locally in Spain since 1513, the Feast of the Holy Name of Mary spread across the ENTIRE world thanks to one unforgettable September morning in **1683**! After two terrifying months under heavy siege, starving **Vienna** looked hours away from falling—until Polish King **Jan III Sobieski** raced across Europe with allied forces, climbed **Kahlenberg Hill** above Vienna at dawn on **September 12, 1683**, served as altar boy himself at Mass offered by **Bl. Marco d’Aviano**, and entrusted the rescue of Central Europe to **the Holy Name of Mary!** That evening, Vienna was freed—and King Sobieski famously sent a humble twist on Julius Caesar’s quote straight to Rome: ***"Venimus, vidimus, Deus vicit!"*** (*"We came, we saw, GOD conquered!"*)

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: When kind old Countess Gutta died, her greedy new daughter-in-law Ottilia fired generous Notburga for feeding poor villagers—ordering leftover castle food dumped to the **pigs** instead! Calmly smiling, Notburga said *"Let God decide!"* and tossed her curved **harvesting sickle** straight up into the air—where legend delights that the **heavy iron sickle hung effortlessly suspended on a golden sunbeam** while the astonished farmer dropped his pitchfork in awe! Hearing of her goodness, repentant Count Henry begged Notburga back to run his entire castle household in justice and charity!

detectiveClues.headline: The Floating Sickle Miracle & Dignity of Rest!
detectiveClues.clueText: When kind old Countess Gutta died, her greedy new daughter-in-law Ottilia fired generous Notburga for feeding poor villagers—ordering leftover castle food dumped to the **pigs** instead! Hired on as a humble field-worker for a nearby peasant farmer, Notburga made ONE joyful condition: **when the Saturday evening church bells rang announcing Sunday rest, she stopped harvesting to pray!** One Saturday, seeing rain clouds coming, her impatient employer ordered her to keep cutting wheat past the prayer bell. Calmly smiling, Notburga said *"Let God decide!"* and tossed her curved **harvesting sickle** straight up into the air—where legend delights that the **heavy iron sickle hung effortlessly suspended on a golden sunbeam** while the astonished farmer dropped his pitchfork in awe! Hearing of her goodness, repentant Count Henry begged Notburga back to run his entire castle household in justice and charity!

stops.imageCaption: Dramatic golden Jerusalem stone gateway where a gleaming Byzantine Emperor removes his jeweled imperial diadem and purple cloak, stepping humbly barefoot in a plain white linen tunic to lift a heavy wooden Cross onto his shoulder.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: That unforgettable scene at Jerusalem’s eastern gate reminds every generation that pride can never carry the Cross—only humility unlocks the door!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: In Greece, Armenia, and across Eastern Europe on **September 14**, priests still adorn the Cross with fresh fragrant **sweet basil (*vasilikos* — literally "royal herb"!)**—because tradition says bright green sweet basil was growing wild all over the exact spot where Empress Helena uncovered the Cross!

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Emperor Heraclius Strips Off His Crown at Jerusalem’s Gate
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Nearly three centuries later, in 614 AD, invading Persian armies captured Jerusalem and carried off the precious relic of the True Cross as a war trophy! After fifteen bitter years, Byzantine **Emperor Heraclius** finally won it back in 628 and marched triumphantly up to **Jerusalem’s Golden Gate** dressed in dazzling gold armor and a jeweled crown, insisting on carrying the Cross up Calvary himself—yet legend tells he suddenly felt **frozen to the cobblestones, unable to take a single step forward!** Stepping beside him, wise Patriarch **St. Zacharias** whispered gently: *"Your Majesty, Jesus didn’t walk this road in jewels and purple silk—He walked it barefoot and humble!"* Immediately weeping, Emperor Heraclius stripped off his crown, gold belt, and royal boots—and walked barefoot in plain linen straight up to Calvary!

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: How did the universal Feast of **Our Lady of Sorrows** spread across Europe? In **1233**, right in the middle of bloody neighborhood clan wars in **Florence**, **seven prosperous Florentine cloth merchants** laid down their wealth and rivalry together, climbed high into the quiet forested peak of **Mount Senario**, and founded the **Servants of Mary (Servites)**! Meditating daily on Mary’s brave, tearful fidelity beneath the Cross (*"Stabat Mater"* — "The Mother stood!"), the Servites popularized devotion to Our Lady of Sorrows as a beacon of compassion and peacemaking across the world!

detectiveClues.headline: Seven Merchants on Forested Mount Senario, Tuscany
detectiveClues.clueText: How did the universal Feast of **Our Lady of Sorrows** spread across Europe? In **1233**, right in the middle of bloody neighborhood clan wars in **Florence**, **seven prosperous Florentine cloth merchants** laid down their wealth and rivalry together, climbed high into the quiet forested peak of **Mount Senario**, and founded the **Servants of Mary (Servites)**! Meditating daily on Mary’s brave, tearful fidelity beneath the Cross (*"Stabat Mater"* — "The Mother stood!"), the Servites popularized devotion to Our Lady of Sorrows as a beacon of compassion and peacemaking across the world!

completionSummary: You sailed across the Yellow Sea with St. Andrew Kim Taegon—Korea’s very first native-born Catholic priest, who was ordained at age 24, smuggled the Gospel back to his homeland on a tiny wooden boat, and stands at the head of 103 heroic Korean martyrs!

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: At **Solmoe Shrine** in Dangjin—honored by Pope Francis in 2014—pilgrims walk peacefully beneath fragrant pines around the lovingly restored traditional *hanok* birthplace of St. Andrew Kim.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Andrew Kim Taegon’s own father, **St. Ignatius Kim**, was martyred while Andrew was studying abroad—making Andrew’s decision to sail straight back into persecuted Joseon Korea an act of jaw-dropping bravery!
stops.saintQuote: We have received baptism and entered the Church—what good is the name of Christian if we do not live it in truth?

stops.title: Writing the Gospel of the Kingdom & Traveling East
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Judea & Ancient Aksum / Ethiopia to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: 1st Century AD · Judea & Ancient Ethiopia / East
stops.imageCaption: Golden afternoon light illuminating an ancient parchment Gospel scroll beside highland stone obelisks and acacia trees where an apostle shares the Beatitudes.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Because Matthew begins his Gospel with Jesus’s human family tree, Christian art symbolizes him with a **Winged Man / Angel**—reminding us that God stepped right into real human history!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Notice a charming accountant’s fingerprint in Matthew’s Gospel? Unlike Mark and Luke, **former tax collector Matthew** uses exact, specialized ancient banking and coinage words—like *talents*, *staters*, and *didrachmas*—including the famous coin found inside a fish’s mouth!
stops.saintQuote: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Why is **Matthew’s Gospel** placed **FIRST** in the New Testament? stops.imageCaption: Warm golden honey-stone Provençal hilltop castle surrounded by fragrant lavender fields, cypress trees, and terraced vineyards glowing under a clear azure sky.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Perched gleaming above Provence’s Luberon vineyards, **Château d’Ansouis** still stands open to visitors—still home to the historic Sabran heritage and the very castle chapel where Elzear and Delphine prayed side by side!

detectiveClues.clueText: Wait—could anyone survive **thirteen straight years** dropped down a dark, freezing **20-foot underground pit**?! Refusing to offer pagan sacrifice to King Tiridates III’s idols, courageous **Gregory** was hurled into the notorious royal dungeon of **Khor Virap** ("Deep Pit") near ancient Artaxata! Year after year, a kind Christian widow secretly tossed a single loaf of bread down the dark shaft each morning—keeping Gregory alive in prayer until the king himself fell gravely ill and his sister dreamed that ONLY the forgotten prisoner in Khor Virap could heal him!
